title: Starting tomatoes from seed
summary: Six to eight weeks before your last frost.
steps: Sow seeds 6 mm (1/4 in) deep, two per cell.
Keep the mix at 21 to 27 °C (70 to 80 °F). Seedlings usually show in 5 to 10 days.
Give them strong light right away; pale, stretched seedlings mean the light is too weak or too far.
Thin to one per cell, and move up to 10 cm (4 in) pots when the first true leaves are fully open.
A small fan on low for an hour a day makes stems sturdier.

title: Planting tomatoes out
summary: Once nights stay above about 10 °C (50 °F).
steps: Harden off for a week first.
Pinch off the lower leaves and plant deep, burying two-thirds of the stem. Roots grow from the buried stem and the plant gets steadier.
Space 60 cm (2 ft) apart in a bed, or one plant per 38 L (10 gal) pot.
Put the stake or cage in now, before roots spread.
Water deeply and mulch with straw to keep soil from splashing onto leaves.

title: Caring for tomatoes through summer
summary: Even water and support make the biggest difference.
steps: Water deeply two or three times a week rather than a little each day; uneven watering causes cracking and blossom end rot.
Tie the main stem to its stake every 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 in) as it grows.
On indeterminate plants, pinch out some of the side shoots that grow between the main stem and a leaf, to keep the plant manageable.
Remove lower leaves that touch the soil or show brown spots.
Check under leaves every few days for hornworms and pick them off.

title: Picking and storing tomatoes
summary: Pick at full color, or a little early to beat pests and heat.
steps: Pick when fruit is fully colored and gives slightly when pressed, or at the first blush of color and let it finish on the counter.
Keep ripe tomatoes at room temperature, out of the sun; the fridge dulls their flavor.
Before the first frost, pick every green tomato with a hint of pale color and ripen them indoors in a box.
For canning, use firm, ripe fruit and a tested recipe; add lemon juice or citric acid as the recipe says.

title: Starting peppers from seed
summary: Eight to ten weeks before the last frost. They are slow, so start early.
steps: Sow 6 mm (1/4 in) deep, two seeds per cell.
Keep the mix warm, 26 to 29 °C (80 to 85 °F), on a heat mat. Seeds can take two weeks to sprout in cooler mix.
Move seedlings under strong light as soon as they appear.
Thin to one per cell and pot up into 10 cm (4 in) pots when they have two or three true leaves.

title: Planting peppers out
summary: Two to three weeks after your last frost, when the soil is warm.
steps: Wait until nights stay above about 13 °C (55 °F); cold nights stall peppers for weeks.
Harden off, then plant 45 cm (18 in) apart at the same depth they grew in the pot.
Stake taller varieties so heavy fruit doesn't snap branches.
Water deeply and mulch.

title: Picking peppers
summary: Green any time, sweeter once colored.
steps: Cut peppers off with scissors or pruners, leaving a short stem; pulling can break branches.
Pick some green early to keep the plant setting more fruit.
For the sweetest flavor, leave peppers until fully colored.
To freeze, wash, seed and slice them; no blanching needed.

title: Starting hot peppers from seed
summary: Eight to ten weeks before the last frost.
steps: Sow 6 mm (1/4 in) deep on a heat mat at 26 to 29 °C (80 to 85 °F).
Super-hot kinds like habanero can take three weeks to sprout; be patient.
Grow under strong light and pot up once there are true leaves.

title: Hot peppers in a pot
summary: One of the best food plants for a container.
steps: Use a pot of at least 11 L (3 gal) with drainage holes and good potting mix.
Set it in full sun after your last frost and the nights have warmed.
Water when the top few centimeters are dry, and feed every two to three weeks.
Before your first fall frost, the pot can come indoors or into the greenhouse to keep producing.

title: Picking and keeping hot peppers
summary: Green or red, fresh, dried or pickled.
steps: Wear gloves when picking and cutting hot kinds, and don't touch your eyes.
Cut, don't pull, leaving a short stem.
Dry thin-walled peppers on a string in a warm, airy spot; store when brittle.
Pickle thick ones like jalapeños with a tested recipe.

title: Starting eggplant from seed
summary: Eight to ten weeks before the last frost.
steps: Sow 6 mm (1/4 in) deep on a heat mat at 24 to 29 °C (75 to 85 °F).
Seedlings appear in one to two weeks. Give strong light right away.
Pot up into 10 cm (4 in) pots after the first true leaves.

title: Planting eggplant out
summary: Wait for real warmth, two to four weeks after the last frost.
steps: Harden off, then plant 60 cm (2 ft) apart.
Cover with row cover right away to keep flea beetles off; remove it when flowers open.
Stake plants once fruit starts to form.

title: Picking eggplant
summary: While the skin is still glossy.
steps: Cut with pruners, leaving a short piece of the green cap on the fruit.
Press the skin: if it springs back, it's ready. Dull skin means it's overripe.
Eggplant keeps only a few days; cook it soon.

title: Planting seed potatoes
summary: Two to four weeks before your last frost.
steps: A week or two ahead, set seed potatoes in a bright, cool room to sprout short green shoots ("chitting").
Cut big potatoes into pieces with at least two eyes each and let the cut sides dry for a day.
Plant 10 cm (4 in) deep and 30 cm (12 in) apart, shoots up, in rows 75 cm (30 in) apart.
In a grow bag, start with 15 cm (6 in) of mix, plant three or four pieces, and cover with 10 cm (4 in).

supplies.name: Seed potatoes
supplies.amount: about 1 kg (2 lb) per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Hilling potatoes
summary: Keep new potatoes covered as the plants grow.
steps: When plants are 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 in) tall, pull soil or mulch up around the stems, leaving the top few leaves showing.
Repeat every couple of weeks until the plants flower.
Water evenly, especially once flowers appear; that's when tubers swell.
Pick off potato beetles and their orange eggs under the leaves.

title: Digging and curing potatoes
summary: Small "new" potatoes in early summer, storage potatoes once the vines die.
steps: For new potatoes, gently feel around the plant two to three weeks after flowering and take a few.
For storage, wait until the tops yellow and die back, then wait two more weeks so the skins toughen.
Dig carefully from the side with a fork to avoid stabbing them.
Brush off soil (don't wash) and cure in a dark, airy spot at about 13 to 16 °C (55 to 60 °F) for two weeks.
Store in the dark at 4 to 10 °C (40 to 50 °F). Keep them away from onions.
Don't eat potatoes with green skin or flesh; the green parts are bitter and can make you sick. Cut away small green spots or compost the potato.
These are low in acid: can them only in a pressure canner with a tested recipe, never in a water bath. Freezing is simpler.

title: Growing your own sweet potato slips
summary: Six to eight weeks before planting out.
steps: Lay a sweet potato on its side in a shallow tray of damp potting mix, half buried, or stand it half in a jar of water.
Keep it warm, about 24 to 29 °C (75 to 85 °F). Shoots appear in two to four weeks.
When shoots are 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 in) long, twist them off and stand them in water until roots form, about a week.

title: Planting sweet potato slips
summary: Two to four weeks after your last frost, in warm soil.
steps: Plant slips 30 cm (12 in) apart in loose, raised rows, burying the stem up to the top leaves.
Water every day for the first week, then only in long dry spells.
Let the vines run; they cover the ground and shade out weeds.

supplies.name: Slips
supplies.amount: about 10 per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Digging and curing sweet potatoes
summary: Before soil turns cold in fall.
steps: Dig about 100 days after planting, or before the soil drops to about 13 °C (55 °F).
Dig wide and carefully; the skins bruise easily.
Cure for 7 to 10 days somewhere warm and humid, about 27 to 32 °C (80 to 90 °F). This sweetens them and heals scrapes.
Store at 13 to 16 °C (55 to 60 °F), never in the fridge. They keep for months.
These are low in acid: can them only in a pressure canner with a tested recipe, never in a water bath. Freezing is simpler.

title: Starting onions from seed
summary: Ten to twelve weeks before you plant them out.
steps: Sow seed thickly in a tray, about 6 mm (1/4 in) deep.
Keep at room temperature until they sprout, then grow under bright light.
Trim the tops back to about 10 cm (4 in) whenever they flop over; it makes thicker seedlings.

title: Planting onion transplants
summary: Two to four weeks before your last frost.
steps: Choose the right day-length type for your latitude (see the plant notes).
Plant 2.5 cm (1 in) deep and 10 cm (4 in) apart in rows 30 cm (12 in) apart.
Water well and keep weeds out; onions can't compete.
Water steadily until the tops start to fall over, then stop.

supplies.name: Onion transplants or sets
supplies.amount: about 30 per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Harvesting and curing onions
summary: When most of the tops have fallen over.
steps: Pull onions on a dry day once most tops have flopped and started to brown.
Lay them in a shady, airy spot for two to three weeks until the necks are dry and papery.
Trim roots and cut tops to 2.5 cm (1 in), or braid the dry tops.
Store in mesh bags somewhere cool, dark and dry. Use thick-necked onions first.

title: Planting garlic in fall
summary: Around your first fall frost, from about two weeks before to two weeks after.
steps: Break bulbs into cloves the day you plant, keeping the papery skins on. Plant the biggest cloves.
Push each clove in pointed end up, 5 cm (2 in) deep and 15 cm (6 in) apart.
Water once, then mulch with 10 cm (4 in) of straw or leaves for the winter.

supplies.name: Seed garlic
supplies.amount: about 0.5 kg (1 lb) per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Harvesting and curing garlic
summary: In early summer, when the lower leaves brown.
steps: Cut off hardneck scapes (curly flower stalks) in spring; they're good to eat.
Stop watering about two weeks before harvest.
Dig when the bottom three or four leaves are brown and the top ones still green.
Hang in bunches or lay out somewhere shady and airy for three to four weeks.
Trim roots and stems and store somewhere cool and dry. Set aside the biggest bulbs to plant in fall.

title: Sowing carrots
summary: From a few weeks before the last frost, and again in late summer for fall.
steps: Loosen soil 30 cm (12 in) deep and remove stones.
Sow 6 mm (1/4 in) deep, about 2 cm (1 in) apart, in rows 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 in) apart.
Keep the surface moist every day for up to three weeks. A board over the row holds moisture; lift it as soon as seedlings show.
Thin to 5 cm (2 in) apart when seedlings are 5 cm tall.

title: Pulling and storing carrots
summary: When the tops of the roots are the width you like.
steps: Brush back soil to check the shoulder width, then pull or loosen with a fork.
Twist off the tops right away so the roots don't go limp.
Store unwashed in damp sand or in bags in the fridge.
Where winters are mild, leave them in the ground under mulch and dig as needed.
These are low in acid: can them only in a pressure canner with a tested recipe, never in a water bath. Freezing is simpler.

title: Sowing beets
summary: From four weeks before the last frost, and again for fall.
steps: Soak seeds for a few hours to speed sprouting.
Sow 1 to 2 cm (1/2 in) deep, 5 cm (2 in) apart.
Each seed is a cluster, so thin to 10 cm (4 in) apart once seedlings are up. Eat the thinnings.

title: Harvesting beets
summary: Golf-ball to tennis-ball size.
steps: Pull when roots are 4 to 8 cm (1.5 to 3 in) across.
Twist off greens, leaving 2.5 cm (1 in) of stem so the roots don't bleed.
Store roots in the fridge or in damp sand; cook greens like chard.

title: Sowing radishes
summary: Every week or two in spring and fall.
steps: Sow 1 cm (1/2 in) deep, 2.5 cm (1 in) apart.
Keep them evenly watered; dry soil makes them hot and woody.
Thin to 5 cm (2 in) apart.

title: Picking radishes
summary: About a month after sowing.
steps: Pull as soon as roots reach full size; they turn pithy if left.
Trim tops and keep the roots in the fridge.

title: Sowing lettuce
summary: In cool weather, a little every two weeks.
steps: Scatter seed thinly and cover with just a sprinkle of soil; lettuce needs light to sprout.
Keep the surface moist until seedlings appear.
Thin leaf lettuce to 15 cm (6 in) and heading types to 25 cm (10 in).
In warm weather, sow where there's afternoon shade.

title: Picking lettuce
summary: Leaf by leaf, or whole heads.
steps: For leaf lettuce, pick outer leaves and leave the center growing.
Cut heads at the base when firm.
Pick in the morning, rinse in cold water and refrigerate.
Pull plants once they start to bolt; the leaves turn bitter.

title: Sowing spinach
summary: Early spring and fall, in cool soil.
steps: Sow 1 cm (1/2 in) deep, 5 cm (2 in) apart.
Thin to 10 cm (4 in).
For winter harvests, cover fall plantings with row cover.

title: Harvesting and freezing spinach
summary: Before the plants bolt.
steps: Pick outer leaves as soon as they're big enough, or cut the whole plant 2.5 cm (1 in) above the soil to let it regrow.
To freeze, blanch leaves for 2 minutes in boiling water, cool in ice water, squeeze dry and bag.

title: Planting kale
summary: A few weeks before the last frost, and again in late summer.
steps: Set transplants 45 cm (18 in) apart, slightly deeper than they grew.
Cover with row cover to keep cabbage moths off.
Water steadily and feed with compost midseason.

title: Picking kale
summary: Leaf by leaf for months.
steps: Pick the lowest leaves when they're about hand-sized, leaving at least the top five or six.
Kale tastes sweeter after a few frosts.
Strip leaves from stems and refrigerate, or blanch and freeze.

title: Planting cabbage
summary: A few weeks before the last frost, or in late summer for fall.
steps: Plant 45 cm (18 in) apart, burying the stem up to the first leaves.
Use row cover against cabbage moths.
Water evenly; uneven water splits heads.

title: Making sauerkraut from your cabbage
summary: Salt and time turn cabbage into a long-keeping ferment.
steps: Shred cabbage finely and weigh it. Mix in 2 teaspoons of salt per 0.5 kg (1 lb) of cabbage.
Squeeze and pound it until it gives off plenty of juice, about 10 minutes.
Pack tightly into a clean jar, pressing until the juice covers the cabbage. Weigh it down.
Cover loosely and leave at cool room temperature for 1 to 4 weeks, tasting along the way.
When it tastes right, close the jar and keep it in the fridge.

supplies.name: A weight to hold the cabbage under the brine

title: Planting broccoli
summary: A few weeks before the last frost, or in late summer for fall.
steps: Plant 45 cm (18 in) apart and water in well.
Cover with row cover against cabbage moths.
Side-dress with compost once heads start to form.

title: Cutting broccoli
summary: When heads are tight and dark green.
steps: Cut the main head with 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 in) of stem before any yellow flowers open.
Leave the plant: side shoots will keep coming for weeks.
To freeze, cut into florets, blanch 3 minutes, cool in ice water and bag.

title: Sowing beans
summary: After the last frost, once the soil is warm.
steps: Wait until the soil is at least 16 °C (60 °F).
Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) apart, in rows 45 cm (18 in) apart.
For pole beans, put up a trellis or teepee first and sow around each pole.
Sow again every three weeks until midsummer for a steady harvest.

supplies.name: Bean seed
supplies.amount: about 30 g (1 oz) per 3 m (10 ft) of row

title: Picking and canning beans
summary: Every few days while pods are slim.
steps: Pick when pods snap cleanly and seeds inside are still small.
Hold the stem with one hand and pull the pod with the other so you don't uproot the plant.
Green beans are low in acid: can them only in a pressure canner with a tested recipe, never in a water bath. Freezing (blanch 3 minutes) is simpler.

title: Sowing peas
summary: Four to eight weeks before the last frost.
steps: Put up the trellis or netting first.
Soak seeds for a few hours, then sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep and 5 cm (2 in) apart along the trellis.
Guide the first tendrils onto the support.

title: Picking peas
summary: Daily once they start.
steps: Pick shelling peas when the pods are plump but still bright green.
Pick snap peas when plump and crisp, snow peas while flat.
Peas lose sweetness fast; shell and freeze the same day (blanch 2 minutes).

title: Sowing cucumbers
summary: One to three weeks after the last frost.
steps: Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, in groups of three, 30 cm (12 in) apart along a trellis.
Thin each group to the strongest plant.
Cover young plants with row cover against cucumber beetles; remove it when flowers appear so bees can reach them.

title: Picking cucumbers and making pickles
summary: Pick small and often.
steps: Pick pickling cucumbers at 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in), slicers at 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 in).
Check every day or two at peak season.
Pickle within a day of picking for the crispest pickles, using a tested recipe.

title: Sowing zucchini
summary: One to three weeks after the last frost.
steps: Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, two seeds per spot, 90 cm (3 ft) apart.
Thin to the stronger seedling.
Mulch well; the big leaves will soon shade the soil.

title: Keeping squash pests in check
summary: A few minutes a week saves the plants.
steps: Look under leaves for clusters of bronze squash bug eggs and scrape them off.
Watch the base of the stem for holes and sawdust-like frass from vine borers.
Water the soil, not the leaves, to slow powdery mildew.
Pick every day or two at peak season.

title: Sowing winter squash
summary: One to three weeks after the last frost.
steps: Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, three seeds per hill, hills 1.2 m (4 ft) apart.
Thin to the two strongest plants per hill.
Give vines room to run, or train them along a fence.

title: Harvesting and curing winter squash
summary: When the rind is hard and the stem has dried.
steps: Harvest when you can't dent the skin with a fingernail, and before a hard frost.
Cut with 5 cm (2 in) of stem; never carry squash by the stem.
Cure in a warm, dry place, about 27 °C (80 °F), for one to two weeks (acorn types skip this).
Store at 10 to 16 °C (50 to 60 °F). Butternut can keep six months or more.
Can only cubes, never mashed squash, and only in a pressure canner with a tested recipe. Freezing cooked purée is simpler.

title: Sowing pumpkins
summary: One to three weeks after the last frost.
steps: Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, three seeds per hill, hills 1.5 m (5 ft) apart.
Thin to two plants per hill.
Slip a board under each pumpkin as it grows to keep it off wet soil.

title: Harvesting and curing pumpkins
summary: When fully colored and the rind is hard.
steps: Cut with a long stem once the color is deep and the rind resists a fingernail.
Cure in a warm, dry spot for about 10 days.
Store cool and dry, and check every few weeks.
Can cubes (not purée) in a pressure canner with a tested recipe, or freeze the purée.

title: Sowing sweet corn in a block
summary: One to three weeks after the last frost, in warm soil.
steps: Wait for soil of at least 16 °C (60 °F).
Sow 2.5 to 5 cm (1 to 2 in) deep, 25 cm (10 in) apart, in at least four short side-by-side rows 75 cm (30 in) apart.
Water deeply, especially when tassels and silks appear.

title: Picking sweet corn
summary: About three weeks after the silks appear.
steps: Ears are ready when the silks are brown and dry and a kernel squirts milky juice when pressed.
Pull down and twist the ear off.
Eat, freeze or can the same day; sugar turns to starch within hours. Corn is low in acid: can it only in a pressure canner with a tested recipe.

title: Sowing okra
summary: Two to four weeks after the last frost, in warm soil.
steps: Soak seeds overnight.
Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, 15 cm (6 in) apart, in soil at least 18 °C (65 °F).
Thin to 40 cm (16 in) apart.

title: Picking okra
summary: Every other day in summer.
steps: Cut pods at 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in), before they turn woody.
Wear gloves and long sleeves.
Pickle, freeze (blanch 3 minutes) or fry.

title: Sowing cowpeas
summary: Two to five weeks after the last frost.
steps: Sow 2.5 cm (1 in) deep, 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) apart, in warm soil.
Water until established; after that they handle dry spells.
Vining types like a fence to climb.

title: Harvesting cowpeas fresh or dry
summary: Green for fresh shelling, brown for dry storage.
steps: For fresh peas, pick when pods have filled out but are still green.
For dry peas, leave pods until they turn brown and rattle, then pick.
Shell, spread out to finish drying, and store in jars somewhere dry.
